question: An operations manager has deliberately kept one chat alive for months, letting Claude condense earlier messages rather than ever starting fresh. What is the biggest concern with this habit?
options: A) A conversation that has been condensed can no longer be exported or shared, so her team is unable to review the thread once it passes the length limit
B) Condensing earlier messages deletes them from her chat history for good, so nobody on the team is able to go back and reread what was originally agreed
C) Automatic condensing is offered only on free accounts, so a paid plan will refuse to shorten the conversation and will simply stop accepting further messages
D) The decisions her team relies on exist only inside one conversation, and Claude now works from a condensed version rather than what was originally agreed
correct_answers: D) The decisions her team relies on exist only inside one conversation, and Claude now works from a condensed version rather than what was originally agreed
explanations: Condensing does not restrict exporting or sharing a conversation; that is unrelated to how context is managed as a chat grows.
Condensing affects what Claude carries forward as working context; the full chat history remains accessible for her to scroll back and read.
Automatic context management is not a free-account-only behaviour, and a conversation reaching its length limit does not simply refuse further messages in the way described.

Correct. Two things go wrong at once: the durable decisions are trapped in a single fragile conversation instead of being persisted somewhere reusable, and once earlier messages are condensed Claude is reasoning from a summary rather than the original wording. Moving what must survive into a Project fixes both.
